treatments.sparse-five:
TASK: Edit the attached photograph by transferring its rendering into sparse black pen lines on white. Treat the photograph as the fixed geometry of the output, not loose inspiration for a newly imagined portrait. Change the rendering medium only. Preserve this exact person's identity, age, pose, expression, facial proportions and natural asymmetry. Do not beautify, average, symmetrize or caricature their features.

ALIGNMENT: Use the supplied image crop as a coordinate map. Keep the same framing, head size, tilt, perspective and margins. At the same image size, the drawing's facial landmarks and observed contours must line up with the photograph when overlaid. Preserve both the position AND shape of the brows, eyelids, nose bridge/tip/nostrils, lips, cheeks, jaw, chin, ears, hairline and glasses if present. Do not move, resize, rotate or reshape individual features. If resolution changes, scale the whole composition uniformly. For a multi-panel sheet, apply only the layout's specified uniform fit and offset to the entire reference within each cell.

EYES: Copy the actual inner and outer eye corners, eyelid curvature, eye opening, tilt, spacing and left/right differences. Preserve the observed gaze and iris/pupil positions where visible, brow shape and brow-to-eye distance. Keep distinctive eyelid folds or under-eye contours when they carry likeness or expression. Use precise observed contour segments; do not replace the eyes with generic almonds, dots, identical arcs or cheerful closed-eye symbols. Do not enlarge, round, open, close or level the eyes, lift the brows, or invent detail hidden by glasses or the pose.

EXPRESSION AND MOUTH: Preserve the exact lip seam, width, curvature, lip thickness, mouth-corner heights and visible opening. A neutral, serious, downturned or closed mouth must stay that way. Preserve a real smile only to the extent present in the photograph. Do not add a smile, raise the mouth corners, expose teeth, part closed lips, lift the cheeks or add a squint to make the person look friendlier. Keep the original expression even if it looks subtle or asymmetric.

PRIORITY: Facial geometry, distinctive features and expression take precedence over every stroke-count, continuity, sparsity or elegance target below. Simplify texture and shading, not the shapes that identify this person. Keep the small contour changes that distinguish their eyes, nose and mouth. If five strokes cannot preserve those features, use additional accurate strokes and pen lifts. Never omit or relocate a defining feature or draw a false connector just to meet a stroke target.

Before returning the image, compare the eye corners and openings, brow heights, nose tip, mouth corners and lip opening, jaw and head silhouette against the source. Correct any shifted landmarks, generic feature substitutions or changed expression. Return only the finished pen drawing; do not include the photograph, an overlay or alignment guides.

LINE TREATMENT:
Create a continuous line sketch with a single-value black line on white. The sketch should be accurate to the picture provided and line up perfectly when overlaid, but be very sparse and gestural, artistic in how it is rendered. The eyes, mouth, nose and face outline are the most important areas to capture; ignore the background. Aim for around five strokes, but use extra accurate strokes wherever needed to preserve the features and expression.

Use one assertive, uniform black pen on a pure white background: constant stroke width and constant ink darkness throughout the entire drawing. Avoid complete outlines, repeated hair strands, geometric eyes, perfect lips, correction marks and connectors through empty space.

LINE TREATMENT:
Use the attached photograph as a fixed reference and reduce the face to only the lines that carry the most identity. Preserve the exact head pose, expression, asymmetry, eye spacing, brow angle, nose shape, mouth shape, jaw, glasses if present, and outer hair silhouette. The finished drawing should still unmistakably resemble the person when viewed small or overlaid on the photograph.

Think like a precise observational draftsman: identify the unusual relationships that distinguish this face from an average face, then preserve those relationships precisely. Do not spend marks on generic anatomy. If a contour does not help recognition, omit it. Prioritize the most characteristic eyebrow and eyelid shapes, the bridge and underside of the nose, the mouth corners and exact lip seam and opening, jaw turns, and the distinctive outer rhythm of the hair.

Aim for about five continuous pen strokes total, using additional accurate strokes when required to preserve the observed features. Each stroke may accomplish several jobs where the reference contours naturally connect. For example, one stroke may follow an eyebrow or eyelid; another may travel from cheek into jaw and neck. Keep features separate wherever connecting them would invent a contour. Allow selective retracing of an existing contour when necessary, but do not create arbitrary connector lines across blank areas merely to keep a stroke alive.

Use a single opaque black line of constant width on pure white, approximately 2–3 pixels at 1024 px. No shading, hatching, gray, tapering, texture, brush effects, dots, individual hairs, individual teeth, filled black shapes or background.

Avoid symbolic or generic facial shorthand: no almond-shaped stock eyes, triangle noses, outlined cartoon lips, symmetrical beautification, complete rings around features, or closed coloring-book contours. The drawing should feel observed rather than designed.

Aim for the economy of a great editorial portrait: very few marks, but every bend in the line should contain information about this specific person. White space should do most of the work.
